# Methods

All three models answer the same question: given what we know about a place before the year starts, how many paid claims should we expect there, per insured home? Let $N_{it}$ be the number of claims in area $i$ and year $t$, $e_{it}$ the number of policy-years, and $\mathbf{x}_{it}$ the facts known in advance (flood zone, coverage, past claims). Each model predicts the expected count $\mu_{it}$, and each takes the number of insured homes into account in the same way, through an offset $\log e_{it}$: twice as many homes means twice as many expected claims, all else equal. The three models receive the same information, so differences in performance come from the models themselves.

## Poisson GLM

$$
N_{it}\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu_{it}),\qquad \log\mu_{it}=\log e_{it}+\mathbf{x}_{it}^\top\boldsymbol\beta
$$ {#eq-poisson}

The Poisson GLM is the textbook model for claim counts. Each feature multiplies the claim rate by a fixed factor, which makes the model easy to read: for example, "homes in V zones file $k$ times more claims than homes in X zones". Its weakness is that it assumes the variance of the counts equals their mean.

## Negative Binomial GLM

$$
\text{Var}(N_{it})=\mu_{it}+\alpha\mu_{it}^2
$$ {#eq-nb}

The negative binomial GLM keeps the same structure as @eq-poisson but lets the variance grow faster than the mean, through an extra parameter $\alpha$. This is exactly what the data show: counts vary about `{python} f"{pearson / df_disp:.0f}"` times more than a Poisson model expects (@fig-eda-dispersion). We expect it to give similar average predictions to the Poisson model, but a more honest picture of their uncertainty.

## LightGBM with Poisson Objective

LightGBM builds hundreds of small decision trees, each one correcting the errors of the previous ones. It uses the same Poisson loss and the same offset as the GLMs, so it predicts the same quantity. The difference is flexibility: the trees can discover on their own that, say, the effect of the flood zone depends on the location, where a GLM would need us to specify this in advance. RQ1 asks whether this flexibility pays off on years the model has never seen. Its settings (size of the trees, learning speed) are tuned on the training years, and a fixed random seed makes the results reproducible.

## Validation

To mimic the real task of predicting the future from the past, settings are chosen by forward validation within 2010 to 2019: train on the earlier years, check on the next one, then move forward one year at a time. The checking years include both stormy years (2016 to 2018) and a quiet one (2019). The final models are then refitted on 2010 to 2019 and evaluated once, on 2020 to 2024.

## Metrics

The metrics are fixed in advance, before looking at the test years, and each answers a different question:

- **Poisson deviance**: how close are the predicted counts to the observed ones overall? Lower is better.
- **Calibration by decile**: grouping areas from least to most risky according to the model, does each group get roughly the number of claims predicted?
- **Gini index**: does the model rank areas in the right order, from safe to risky? This matters most for pricing, and it does not depend on the overall level of the predictions.
- **Predicted versus observed totals per test year**: how far off is the model in each hurricane year?

Results are reported overall and separately for Florida and the other seven states (RQ2). As a check, the models are also refitted on all claims rather than paid claims only.

# Findings and Discussion

No model has been fitted yet, but the exploration already tells us what to expect.

**All models will predict too few claims in the test years.** The frequency rises from `{python} f"{kn['freq_train']:.1f}"` claims per 1,000 policy-years in 2010 to 2019 to `{python} f"{kn['freq_test']:.1f}"` in 2020 to 2024 (@fig-eda-years). A model calibrated on the first decade cannot anticipate Ian or Helene. This supports H3, and the totals per year will show how large the gap is.

**Ranking places by risk will be the real test.** Because the places hit change from one decade to the next (@fig-eda-persistence), even the ranking of areas will be hard to get right. LightGBM could gain by finding finer patterns, or lose by fitting too closely to the storms of the 2010s; the Gini index and the calibration by decile are designed to tell which.

**Florida is the case to watch.** It looked relatively safe in the training years and was hit hardest in the test years (@tbl-freq-state). Reporting Florida separately (RQ2) will show whether a model's apparent success or failure comes from a single state.

**The two GLMs should look alike.** With the same structure for the mean, they should give close predictions (H2); the negative binomial model should mainly describe the uncertainty better, given how dispersed the counts are.
